articles.headline: The Foot and Mouth Disease Scare.
articles.text:
The Texas Live Stock Journal publishes a complete exposure of the Kansas foot and mouth disease scare. Some of the best veterinary surgeons of the United States and Canada who have had much experience with the disease in England and who have made careful examinations in Kansas, have been interviewed and they all state positively that there has not been a symptom of the foot and mouth disease. The whole trouble was caused by allowing the animals to stand in filth and decaying vegetation, which generated large amounts of ammonia. This inflamed the hoofs and made them freeze easily. Much of the hay fed was wild rye upon almost every stalk of which ergot was clinging. This generated a disease called ergotism which draws the blood from the extremities. This disease further increased the tendency to freeze the feet, and to the above causes, the whole shameful scare can be attributed. With good cause we can say the scare was shameful, for it has done the live stock of the United States infinite pecuniary damage, and was the result in the first place of gross ignorance both of the disease itself and how to take care of cattle.

This leads us to speak of a subject which we have had in mind for a long time. It is that the government should appoint a competent corps of veterinary surgeons who should immediately take charge and have under complete control infected cattle. In Germany, for instance, every hamlet almost has a veterinary surgeon to whom every head of infected stock must be reported. He is the supreme arbitrator in all cases, and if he considers the disease contagious or the animal beyond recovery, he immediately orders it killed and the body disposed of in such a way that infection is impossible from the carcass. A fund is established by the German government and for every animal thus killed the owner receives about two-thirds the value. Long experience has proved that this is the only sure way to prevent contagion, and that the plan is eminently successful.

On the other hand, in the United States, the owner suffers a complete loss in case the animal dies and by keeping it until the last hope of its living has expired many others are liable to be infected. Should the government take hold of the matter and establish a fund and a corps of competent veterinarians all danger of a repetition of the Kansas scare would be over.

We call the attention of stockmen to this idea and hope that future meetings of the different associations will take immediate measures to have the project pushed. It is the only effective way in which our stock can be protected from groundless rumors of infection.
articles.summary: Editorial calling the Kansas foot-and-mouth scare groundless and urging a government veterinary corps and indemnity fund.

articles.text: There has been considerable comment of late among stock papers as to the advisability of shipping dressed meat to Europe. They one and all approve the idea. It does, in fact, seem hard to bring any objection to the plan, and we hope soon to see the matter thoroughly tested. The Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Co. has already demonstrated that there is a large profit in killing cattle and shipping the dressed meat to market. This is owing to the fact that all the shrinkage, which live stock experiences in being taken to market alive, is saved by the refrigerator plan, there is much less trouble and expense in handling and from a third to a half is saved in freight charges. Exactly the same reasons will make it profitable to kill cattle in or near the range and ship the dressed meat to Europe. It has been satisfactorily demonstrated that meat dressed in New York can be shipped to Europe at a large profit, so that it is absolutely certain that a much larger profit could be realized by killing the cattle on the range. In fact, the additional profit would be exactly the profit that is now made by shipping dressed instead of live meat to New York. The Northern Pacific Refrigerator Car Co. is one of the most enterprising as it will soon be the largest concern of the kind in the world, and we hope to see it take the initiative in this new departure.
articles.summary: Editorial urging that range-killed dressed beef be shipped to Europe, with the N. P. Refrigerator Car Co. taking the lead.

articles.text: This will be the last issue in which we can call attention to the meeting for forming a Bad Lands stock association to be held here next Monday. Since the call was framed several other and very important reasons have arisen in addition to all those presented before, why we should have a first-rate organization here. Perhaps the most important one is that the Glendive association has been abandoned. This makes the nearest association that of Miles City, too far away for members to take particular interest in Bad Lands stock. After we are started, however, we can easily join forces with Miles City and thus form a very strong association. In addition to this, is the fact that the Bad Lands stockmen need some special legislation which only concerns themselves and would be of no interest to another association. Starting now, too, we would be the only association of the kind in Dakota, and it would be a very easy matter to make this point the headquarters for Dakota stockmen. The greatest point of all, however, when it comes to a realization, will be found in the new Medora-Black Hills railroad. This will make Medora the market for the immense stock interests of the Black Hills and all the Bad Lands south of here. For these reasons, in addition to the patent advantages a good association confers upon its members we confidently look forward to next Monday for the inauguratson of one of the best stock associations in the whole west. Every stockman who consults his own interests will be present. The meeting will be held at 2 P. M. at the Hotel de Mores.
articles.summary: Editorial urging stockmen to attend Monday's meeting at the Hotel de Mores to form a Bad Lands stock association.

articles.text: Were it not for the fact that our Dickinson correspondent is abundantly able to take care of himself in his spat with the editor of The Press, we would be tempted to make a few remarks. As it is we will merely state that in the first place our correspondent took exception to an advertisement of Dickinson which stated that a thousand teams were employed on the freight route from that point. From the mass of school-boy drivel that this article occasioned in The Press we extract the meaning that the advertisement concerning the thousand teams was truthful. We don't propose to argue the question, but would say that common sense should teach any one that such a baseless fabrication would only react as a boomerang on the town. There is such a thing as legitimate booming, but it should not be confounded with downright lying. Our correspondent had the interests of Dickinson at heart when he took exception to the senseless statement of the advertisement. Its purpose was certainly to gain settlers for Dickinson. Suppose it succeeded in getting them there, who can doubt that they would be utterly disgusted at the outset. Our correspondent was exactly right when he said: "The simple truth about this country when it becomes known, will bring men and means to develop it quite as rapidly as is consistent with a healthy growth."
articles.summary: Editorial backing the Cow Boy's Dickinson correspondent in his quarrel with the Dickinson Press over a 'thousand teams' freight advertisement.

articles.headline: Republican County Convention.
articles.text:
The Republicans of Billings county met pursuant to call last Saturday afternoon at the Hotel de Mores. The meeting was called to order by A. T. Packard, who nominated J. C. Fisher for chairman. The motion was seconded and carried unanimously. Fred Ertel moved that A. T. Packard be elected secretary. Carried unanimously.

By request of the chairman, Mr. Ertel stated the object of the meeting, to elect a delegate to the Huron convention and a county central committee.

A. T. Packard moved that Fred Ertel be appointed delegate to the Huron convention. Carried unanimously.

The county central committee was then elected as follows: J. C. Fisher, Max Bass, A. T. Packard, Geo. Blankenberg, H. Gilbert.

Fred Ertel then offered the following resolutions, which were unanimously adopted:

WHEREAS, The time for filling the vacancy caused by the expiration of Gov. Ordway's term is drawing near and it is important that an executive who is fully conversant with the needs and wants of the people of Dakota be appointed.

Resolved, that in Col. C. A. Lounsberry, of Bismarck, the Republicans of Billings county see a man in every way qualified to assume the high responsibilities of said office; a man in whom the greatest confidence can be placed, a man whose long residence in the territory and past honorable career entitle him to the unqualified confidence of every citizen in the same. Col. Lounsberry is a recognized leader among leaders and has at all times been found foremost when the welfare of the territory has been at stake. The Republicans of Billings county recognize in him a thorough representative of the territory, a staunch Republican, a wise and experienced legislator, a gentleman of highest character and heartily endorse his candidacy for the honorable office to be made vacant.

Resolved, That a copy of these resolutions be transmitted to the president of the United States for his most careful consideration.

WHEREAS, The territory of Dakota is and for some years has been badly handicapped by the government discriminating against the purchaser of public lands within the railroad limits by charging him $2.50 per acre against only $1.25 when outside said limit.

WHEREAS, The completion of the N. P. R. R. has opened up for settlement a vast area of public domain, consisting of the most fertile soil, which suffers under this apparent unjust discrimination, especially at a time when the eyes of emigration are particularly directed to this section.

WHEREAS, A bill has been introduced in congress by Maj. Strait, of Minnesota, to reduce the price of public lands within the railroad limits from $2.50 to $1.25 per acre, be it

Resolved, That the Republicans of Billings county, in convention assembled, heartily endorse the bill as introduced by Mr. Strait.

Resolved further, That the delegate of Billings county to the territorial convention, to be held at Huron, April 23, 1884, be hereby instructed to use his utmost endeavors to urge upon the members of said convention the great benefit derived by the passage of said bill, and if possible secure their aid to direct the attention of congress to the importance of this bill and pray for an early passage of the same.

A. T. Packard moved that the county central committee be empowered to collect money to defray the expenses of the Huron delegate. Carried.

Fred Ertel moved that the thanks of the meeting be tendered to G. W. Fitzgerald for the use of his room. Carried.

Adjourned.

J. C. FISHER, Chairman.
A. T. PACKARD, Secretary.
articles.summary: Minutes of the Billings County Republican convention at the Hotel de Mores, which named Fred Ertel delegate to Huron and endorsed C. A. Lounsberry for governor.

articles.headline: Round-Up.
articles.text:
The cattlemen of the Hills ranges whose headquarters are in Rapid City, met at that place on April 1 and organized for the round-up, by electing two foremen, Wm. Moses and H. Hood, and Jones, Driskill, Coleman and Criswell as assistants.

Stockmen who do not belong to the association, and ranchmen who own cattle that have gone off to the herds should be ready and join with the boys when they start out. They can by so doing, not only get their cattle, but at the same time have a good time.

The following is the programme agreed upon, and that will be followed out to the letter:

No. 1. On June 1, to commence at the mouth of Elm creek on the Belle Fourche, work up the Belle Fourche and all its tributaries to the mouth of Cabin creek. Wm. Moses, foreman; Jones and Driskill, assistants.

No. 2. On June 1, to commence at the head of the Box Elder, work to the mouth of the Box Elder on the Little Missouri; thence up all its tributaries to the head of the Little Missouri. H. Hood, foreman; Coleman and Criswell, assistants.
—[Black Hills Times.
articles.summary: Black Hills Times report of the Rapid City round-up organization and the June 1 round-up plan reaching the Little Missouri.

articles.headline: STOCK NOTES. Call for Bad Lands Association.
articles.text:
There will be a meeting held at Little Missouri crossing, the third Monday in April (the 21st) for the purpose of forming a Bad Lands Association. All raisers of live stock are requested to attend. Upon its organization, business of much importance will come before the association and it is to the interest of every man interested in live stock to attend.
THE COMMITTEE.
articles.summary: Standing call for the April 21 meeting to form a Bad Lands stock association.

articles.headline: Stock Notes
articles.text:
The fright about the foot and mouth disease has about subsided, but reports that have gone to England and other countries can never be recalled, and it is undoubtedly true that damage to the extent of hundreds of thousands of dollars has been done to Kansas, and the live-stock trade of the whole country has suffered incalculable loss on that account. The matter has served a good purpose in arousing the country to the need of taking ample measures for the suppression and prevention of any calamity that might arise in future.

There are 50,000 head of cattle in the Comanche County Pool, Kansas.

There are now 4,000 head of cattle on the Cantrell ranch on the Gila. This herd was purchased and put upon the range last year, and no increase was expected until this spring. There has been however, 800 head of calves belonging to this herd branded. Of this large increase only two have been lost.—[Colfax, N. M., Stockman.

Lately we made some inquiries as to the experiment of breeding Polled Angus and Galloway bulls to our range cows, scrubs and high grades, and are agreeably surprised to learn that in every instance the ranchman has been successful and is preparing to further test the virtues claimed for the black muleys. Perhaps the most extensive tests being made are by the firm of Hunter & Evans, who have a large fenced range in this county, well stocked and carefully looked after, and the Comanche Pool, with its 50,000 head of cattle. Hunter & Evans have on their place about fifty head of heifers, coming two years old this spring, bred from high-bred Short-horn cows and Polled Angus and Galloway bulls, and many of these are in calf from a thoroughbred imported Galloway bull, and will this spring drop three-quarter bred calves. Besides the heifers mentioned above, this firm also raised about sixty bulls, the same as the heifers, and these were sold to the Comanche Pool last year and turned loose on their range. From the time these calves were dropped until now they have done well every day, readily taking to the range diet, adapting themselves to heat and cold as though neither was objectionable, "rustling" by the side of Texans, and still maintaining flesh, strength and energy. They were nearly every one black and in every instance hornless, showing that the stronger blood was in their sires and predominated. The heifers are well filled out and promise a good crop of calves. The bulls turned in the Comanche Pool pasture are wintering in splendid shape, are no trouble whatever and even now are more active than their Short-horn cousins. It is confidently expected that quite a sprinkling of black muley calves will be discovered following the cows on this range even this season, and by next spring the result of these sixty industrious animals will undoubtedly be an attraction. Those gentlemen in the east who are handling either the Galloways or the Polled Angus cattle need not hesitate to warrant these breeds will stand the range under all circumstances with any horned breed, and that a cross from them with a Texas or grade cow will be as good an animal as can be bred for the range.—[Barber County, Kan., Index.

It is estimated that there are at this time fully 2,500 head of horses on this market. The demand for cow ponies has fallen off and prices range from $25 to $40. Most of the heavy buyers have been supplied. There will probably be from ten to twelve thousand stock horses and mares driven this season, the bulk of which will go to Dodge.—[San Antonio Cor. Texas Live Stock Journal.

As the time draws near when preparations begin for the calf crop of 1885, we would again call the attention of our range cattlemen to the necessity of having with their herds a full supply of vigorous bulls. Bulls that have size, form, constitution and merit. High grades we believe to be the best, but if these cannot be had in numbers and condition sufficient to meet the entire demand of the herd, then get the best native bulls to be had, and above all things be careful to have enough on the range to serve every female old enough to produce a calf. Do not emulate the custom so many have indulged in of depending on roving bulls of neighboring ranchmen to make calves for you, but talk to all holding near your ranch, and by united effort put on the ranges as many bulls as are required. We are assured that more than [90?] per cent of calves can be annually secured in any part of Texas, if the cows are all served. Then see to it, now, before breeding begins that your herds are fully supplied with good bulls, lusty fellows and vigorous animals. You will find the money expended in this way will pay better than in any other.—[Texas L. S. Journal.
articles.summary: Stock Notes column of clipped range items: end of the foot-and-mouth scare, Comanche Pool, Gila herd, Polled Angus and Galloway crosses in Kansas, Texas horse market, and bull supply.

articles.headline: DICKINSON NOTES.
articles.text:
DICKINSON, April 16, 1884.

The examination of Joseph McClung, which attracted much attention from the gravity of the charge against him, resulted as was expected, in his discharge.

Asa Fisher has bought the Seaman corner and R. L. Wright will occupy the place. Mr. Fisher is to be congratulated upon having secured a valuable property.

Jerry Russell arrived from St. Paul last week with a car-load of stock and farm implements. He also brought furniture for his livery stable.

The stable and office erected by Matt. Kincaid are nearly ready for business and will form an acquisition to the business interests of the town.

Mr. Anderson opened his new place last week. The bowling alley will be reported for business in a few days.

There has been a little talk of organizing a base-ball nine among the young men here. It is thought that Dickinson could produce a fair team.

A large quantity of Black Hills freight was side-tracked here on Monday.

While we do not wish to prolong a fruitless controversy, at the same time being in, we would not appear to shrink from the contest. Therefore, we will say to The Press that vituperation is not argument. Instead of touching our position on the question of commercial ethics, it dives to the bottom of a putrid inkwell, stirs up a vile cloud and hides like a cuttle fish under cover of its own excretion. Aside from the manner, the matter of The Press criticism is equally ineffective, irrelevant and insincere. We have to charge it with publishing an intentional untruth in its hopeless attempt to distract attention from the real point. It is unfortunate that our E. C. is not willing to advocate the cause of honesty in business methods.
ANTHROPOS.
articles.summary: Dickinson correspondence: McClung discharged, property sales, new businesses, Black Hills freight, and a reply to the Dickinson Press.

articles.text:
Smoke the Far West.

City lots for sale at this office.

A trial of the Far West cigar is its best recommendation.
articles.summary: Brief puffs for the Far West cigar and city lots for sale at the Cow Boy office.

articles.text: The Marchioness de Mores is expected here in a week or ten days.
articles.summary: The Marchioness de Mores is expected in Medora within a week or ten days.

articles.text: Bob Roberts has gone to Miles City to attend court, now in session there.
articles.summary: Bob Roberts has gone to Miles City for court.

articles.text: The Far West is the best cigar in the city. The Senate holds the sole agency.
articles.summary: Puff for the Far West cigar at the Senate.

articles.text: Geo. Roderick began breaking yesterday afternoon on the butte east of town.
articles.summary: Geo. Roderick began breaking ground on the butte east of town.

articles.text: Maj. Snider and Doc Pennell left for Spearfish Monday.
articles.summary: Maj. Snider and Joe ('Doc') Pennell left for Spearfish.

articles.text: A. J. Rich and G. W. Randall came in Monday evening for a week's visit to Howard Eaton.
articles.summary: A. J. Rich and G. W. Randall arrived to visit Howard Eaton.

articles.text: Dr. Duncan, of Glendive, last evening passed through on his way west. He will be here to-morrow or Saturday.
articles.summary: Dr. Duncan of Glendive passed through, to return Friday or Saturday.

articles.text: Wise & Goodkind, of Bismarck, have given Roberts & Co. the sole right to sell the Far West cigar in Little Missouri.
articles.summary: Roberts & Co. gets the sole Far West cigar agency.

articles.text: A telegram from Mr. Peter Book, as we go to press, states that he will be here Saturday with his men and machinery.
articles.summary: Brickmaker Peter Book will arrive Saturday with men and machinery.

articles.text: Several cattle were killed by a freight last Saturday morning west of town. The Northern Pacific is good for them.
articles.summary: Several cattle killed by a freight train west of town.

articles.text: A number of coal miners have arrived and it is expected that the mine will be in full operation by the first of next month.
articles.summary: Coal miners have arrived; mine expected in full operation by May 1.

articles.text: We hope all our stockmen will heed the call for the meeting next Monday. It will be held at 2 P. M. at the Hotel de Mores.
articles.summary: Reminder of Monday's stockmen's meeting at the Hotel de Mores.

articles.text: Rev. Wm. Cooke preached very acceptably last Sunday at the Cantonment. He will hold regular services there every Sunday evening.
articles.summary: Rev. Wm. Cooke preached at the Cantonment and will hold Sunday evening services.

articles.text: Mr. A. H. Morrison, N. P. R. R. auditor, was here Monday looking over Mr. Spurrier's accounts. It is needless to say that they were all right.
articles.summary: N. P. auditor A. H. Morrison checked agent Spurrier's accounts.

articles.text: The thanks of the Republican convention to Geo. Fitzgerald for the use of his room were very fitting. A better place could not be found.
articles.summary: Praise for G. W. Fitzgerald's room used by the Republican convention.

articles.text: Howard Eaton's usual happy smile was wonderfully augmented last Saturday. We didn't blame him when we saw his mother and sister step from the cars.
articles.summary: Howard Eaton's mother and sister arrived by train.

articles.text: "Ox-Bow Jack," alias Johnny Goodall, started west last evening to buy about a hundred head of horses to be used on the round-up. His first stop will be at Terry.
articles.summary: Johnny Goodall went west to buy round-up horses.

articles.text: Two young gentlemen of the west side are breeding a violent sickness. They are assured that the next pies they rustle won't have near as an agreeable effect on them.
articles.summary: Joke about two young men who stole pies.

articles.text: The petition for the survey of this township which was circulated recently, met with almost unanimous approval and we hope the surveyor general will act upon it immediately.
articles.summary: Petition for a township survey widely signed.

articles.text: We doubt if more business will ever be done more quickly or harmoniously than at the Republican convention last Saturday. There was not a hitch in the proceedings and the meeting augered well for concerted action of the party in the future.
articles.summary: Comment on the harmonious Republican convention.

articles.text: The recent rains have gladdened the hearts of the stockmen. The grass started up beautifully about two weeks ago, but the dry weather had a depressing effect on it. The rains of the last few days have given it a fresh and sufficient start so that it is now growing rapidly.
articles.summary: Recent rains restored the range grass.

articles.text: Mr. R. E. Spurrier, agent of the N. P. R. R. at this point, has resigned his position to take effect May 1. He expects to go to Spokane Falls as operator, and was led to make the change in order that his daughter's education might not be neglected. His many friends will regret seeing him go.
articles.summary: N. P. agent R. E. Spurrier resigns effective May 1.

articles.text: The Mandan Pioneer publishes the following as though it were a fact: "The Dickinson Press says that there are about 400,000 pounds of freight lying there for transportation to the Black Hills, and that Medora has not a pound yet." We see that you are not acquainted with the editor of The Press, Bro. Tuttle.
articles.summary: Rebuttal of a Dickinson Press claim about Black Hills freight, reprinted by the Mandan Pioneer.

articles.text: Mrs. Samuel English arrived Saturday night. For the present Mr. and Mrs. English will live at the Cantonment. Mrs. English is not in very good health, but this climate is sure to bring her health back. Mr. English will soon open a general commission store, selling fruit, fish, etc. It will be a needed addition.
articles.summary: Mrs. Samuel English arrived; Mr. English to open a commission store.

articles.text: That we will have a stage line in addition to our freight line is now beyond all question. Mr. Nye, of Livingston, Mont., was here the first of the week and is eager to at once enter upon the preliminary steps toward putting on a line of stages. The only question is, whether Mr. Nye or the company will put them on.
articles.summary: Mr. Nye of Livingston plans a stage line from Medora.

articles.text: As the season approaches for the annual awakening to duty of the deadly massasauger, or prairie rattlesnake, whose bite is almost certain death, Mr. James Hannigan is about to confer a boon on an appreciative public. He has a cure which is warranted in every case to destroy all evil effect on the person bitten. The cure comes in liquid form in pint and half-pint bottles.
articles.summary: Joke puff for James Hannigan's liquid snakebite 'cure'.

articles.text: Lots are going off in good shape. They have only been on the market a few days but already over fifty have been bought or reserved. As soon as word comes that final arrangements have been made to build the railroad to the Hills, the lots will start on a boom that will soon take away the choicest bargains. Come to THE COW BOY office, examine the plat and invest before it is everlastingly too [illegible]
articles.summary: Over fifty Medora town lots sold or reserved in a few days.

articles.text: Messrs. Hines & Casey, of Glendive, left yesterday for home. We are pleased to state that before leaving they made arrangements to open a drug store here within a week or two. For the present they will rent the room now occupied by the N. P. Ref. Car Co. as a meat market. They will soon erect a building of their own. We are glad to welcome the new firm and predict for them a successful future. Mr. Casey will probably have charge of the store here.
articles.summary: Hines & Casey of Glendive will open a drug store in Medora.

articles.text: Three car-loads of Black Hills freight arrived Tuesday morning and the first trip will doubtless be made as soon as Joe Pennell returns from Deadwood. Telegrams have been received from nearly every large dealer in the Hills that every pound of their freight shall be shipped from here. Deadwood merchants are greatly interested in our railroad and will do anything in their power to bring it to completion. Their first action was a concerted movement to have all their freight shipped via Medora, which assures the complete success of our freight route.
articles.summary: Three car-loads of Black Hills freight arrived for the Medora-Deadwood route.

articles.text: G. W. Racek, the well-known saddler and harness maker of Bismarck, came in last evening. His intention is to start a harness shop here and he will make a specialty of cow boy outfits. There is not a better opening on the line and Mr. Racek has shown his energy and foresight by taking the first chance. He bought one lot of us and reserved three others, which also goes to prove his level-headedness. He will erect a substantial brick building as soon as Mr. Book can get the brick ready for him. He returned to Bismarck to-day to settle up his business there.
articles.summary: Bismarck saddler G. W. Racek will open a harness shop in Medora.

articles.text: M. Adolph Eyraud, the Marquis' gardener, is making many improvements in the bottom south of the Marquis' house. A large number of hot beds are doing well and the work of transplanting has just begun. Ten acres have been broken and twenty more will be soon. Two experienced New Jersey gardeners, the Sigler brothers, arrived lately and are lending valuable aid. M. Eyraud expects in addition to the garden, to grow a large number of grapes. If the season is not too short they will be a success, as the bottom land will certainly be warm enough.
articles.summary: The Marquis' gardener Adolph Eyraud is developing a large garden south of the Marquis' house.

articles.text: It would have melted the risibilities of Sitting Bull to have seen Mr. Paddock fit Mr. Allen to a pair of "chapps" last Monday evening. It wouldn't have been in consonance with Bad Lands human nature if such an opportunity for fun had been allowed to escape, and the look of intense earnestness on Mr. Paddock's face as he carefully pulled the "chapps" over Mr. Allen's "dips" wrong side to, would have broken the heart of a stoic. Every one was "on" except the victim, who thought that the hip pockets were rather unhandy. At last the "chapps" were put on right, Mr. Paddock carefully tied one of Mr. Allen's feet to the stirrup and as Messrs. Jones and Allen dashed off in the direction of Deadwood in the rain and darkness, the voice of the latter was heard calling back: "Well, boys, if you've had any fun with me, I'm glad of it."
articles.summary: E. G. Paddock's joke putting chaps on F. B. Allen backwards before Allen and Jones rode for Deadwood.

articles.text: Marquis de Mores and Joe Pennell started yesterday morning at 4:30 for Deadwood. There were three relays of horses sent on ahead, and they expect to make the 185 miles in thirty-six hours. Messrs. Allen and Jones started the night before, and at Deadwood they will complete arrangements for the railroad. There is no doubt whatever that they mean business as the plan is entirely feasible and will certainly be a very paying investment. Plenty of capital is already guaranteed and the only question is as to an agreement on the final arrangements. The railroad will tap the best mining, agricultural and stock country in the United States, and it will probably pay from the send-off. We hope to chronicle the fact that all arrangements have been completed, in our next issue.
articles.summary: The Marquis de Mores and Joe Pennell set out for Deadwood to arrange a Medora-Black Hills railroad.

articles.text: Monday morning we sold four $250 lots to the Merchant's National Bank, of Deadwood. As soon as brick can be received a substantial brick building will adorn the corner of Third street and Broadway. Meantime it is expected that the bank will do business in some of the company's buildings. The bank firm, Stebbins, Mund & Co., is known as the largest and soundest banking firm in the whole Northwest, and our citizens can be congratulated on having such a sound institution start here. With Mr. Fox as another partner, this firm has banks at Deadwood, Spearfish, Lead City, Billings and Livingston, Mont. The bank here is its latest venture and its establishment will speak in the loudest terms, the future of Medora. This firm is too careful and experienced to invest thousands of dollars in real estate and buildings unless there was a certainty of success.
articles.summary: Merchant's National Bank of Deadwood bought four lots to open a Medora bank.

articles.text: Major Wm. R. Snider, editor of the Spearfish Register, made us a pleasant visit Monday. He comes direct from Washington, where he has been on business. He reports that, contrary to general opinion, the Northwestern road never has been granted the right of way across the Sioux reservation and that as the bill for the opening of the reservation is so far down on the calendar there is no chance whatever that it will be acted on at this session of congress. Even when the reservation is opened it will be very doubtful if the Northwestern will build into the Hills, as their policy, although liberal, is against building a line through such an extent of, at present, unproductive country. This leaves an open field for a railroad from Medora and it will undoubtedly be begun very soon. Men are at present interested in the project who have plenty of money and who mean business. The cost of building the entire road from here will not exceed twice the amount that it will take for a Chicago road to bridge the big Missouri and Cheyenne. About half the way there is such a level grade that absolutely no more work will be required than to lay the track. Our readers can rest assured that a railroad from here to the Hills is a thing of the very near future.
articles.summary: Spearfish editor Wm. R. Snider visited and reported no rival Northwestern line to the Hills was imminent.

articles.headline: BELFIELD GOSSIP.
articles.text:
BELFIELD, Dak., April 16, 1884.
EDITOR COW BOY:

Quite a delegation from Belfield attended the Republican convention at Medora on Saturday last. They report a pleasant time and a harmonious meeting.

Rev. R. H. Fulton held divine services in the Presbyterian church last Sunday. The probabilities are that he will be permanently located at this place; at any rate it is sincerely hoped so.

Brace Gallien has returned from the east and is now making preparations to do farming on a large scale.

Two good and substantial settlers arrived this morning from Chicago, bringing with them a car-load of household goods, stock, farming implements, etc., and are exceedingly well prepared to endure the hardships characteristic of the settler's first year's residence.

Mr. Max Bass is having plans made for an addition to his popular hotel and otherwise making preparations for the large immigration which Belfield is soon to witness,

Louis C. Hay has been sojourning in Mandan the past few days. He is expected home this evening.

Parties are looking over the ground for the establishment of a brickyard here, and numerous brick buildings will undoubtedly decorate our town in the near future.
SADIE.
articles.summary: Belfield correspondence: convention delegation, Presbyterian services, settlers from Chicago, Max Bass hotel addition, brickyard plans.
